template_name: Material Aging and Temporal Depth — Patina as Perceptual Enrichment

mechanism_chain.process: Occupant perceives material aging features: patina (oxidation colour change on copper, bronze), wear patterns (polished stone thresholds, smooth wood handrails), weathering (lichen on stone, grain exposure on wood), staining (use patterns, water marks). These are multi-sensory: visual (colour change, texture modification), haptic (smoothing from use, roughening from weather), olfactory (aged wood scent differs from new wood).
mechanism_chain.substrate: Multi-sensory material perception (same pathway as MATERIAL_IDENTITY_INTEGRATION_001) with temporal feature extraction

data: Patina (oxidation): copper green, bronze brown (visual + chemical signature)
Wear patterns: polished stone thresholds, smooth wood handrails (visual + haptic smoothing)
Weathering: lichen on stone, grain exposure on wood (visual + haptic roughening)
Staining: use patterns, water marks, UV bleaching (visual temporal signature)
Olfactory aging: aged wood scent differs from new wood (volatile profile changes)
justification.backing: Mikellides (1990) empirical study of material aging perception. Pallasmaa (2005) phenomenological framework. Materials science (Zuo et al., 2015) on patina formation and aging kinetics.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.5 reflects field observation and psychophysical measurement. EMPIRICAL_COVARIANCE warrant: aging features are measured and correlate with time.
justification.rebuttal: Aging features can be artificially induced (artificial patina, distressed finishes), suggesting perceptual cues are separable from actual age. Some occupants may perceive aging as deterioration rather than enrichment.
competing_accounts: Aging is primarily visual degradation: partially true but haptic smoothing and olfactory signature are distinct channels
Aging perception is purely learned (expectation): refuted by infant and non-human animal responses to textural complexity, suggesting perceptual salience
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Mikellides empirical authority; Pallasmaa theoretical

mechanism_chain.process: Aging features are perceptually categorized as 'temporal depth indicators' — evidence that the material has existed over time and has been used by others. This temporal information is extracted automatically: the visual system detects wear patterns, patina, and weathering as statistical deviations from 'new' material appearance.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Visual temporal feature extraction (texture analysis); somatosensory wear-pattern detection

data: Visual temporal feature extraction: wear patterns detected by texture analysis (statistical deviation from new material)
Somatosensory wear-pattern detection: smoothing of high-friction surfaces is detectable through haptic exploration
Patina and weathering are statistical outliers in material appearance databases
Temporal depth is automatically inferred by visual system without conscious deliberation
justification.backing: Pallasmaa (2005) on phenomenological 'existential anchoring'. Mikellides (1990) on automatic perceptual categorization. Visual texture analysis literature (Portilla & Simoncelli, 2000) on texture statistics extraction.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.45 reflects theoretical framework and field observation but limited direct evidence. CAPACITY warrant: functional capacity to extract temporal features is inferred from behavioral outcomes.
justification.rebuttal: Temporal depth inference requires prior knowledge of 'new' material baseline; unfamiliar materials may not trigger this inference. Some occupants may not extract temporal information consciously.
competing_accounts: Aging perception is purely cultural learning (partially true; cultural context modulates baseline but perceptual salience of texture changes is pre-cultural)
Temporal depth is conscious deliberation only (refuted by rapid implicit categorization of aged vs. new materials)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Pallasmaa theoretical framework

mechanism_chain.process: Temporal depth indicators activate evaluative responses: aged materials are rated as more 'authentic,' 'characterful,' and 'trustworthy' than pristine equivalents (Mikellides, d ≈ 0.40–0.60). Pallasmaa's theoretical framework interprets this as 'existential anchoring' — connection to the continuity of human habitation.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Orbitofrontal evaluation; possible interaction with social cognition (inferring others' use-history)

data: Aged materials rated 0.40-0.60 SD higher on authenticity and character (Mikellides, 1990)
Authenticity effect persists across European cultural contexts
Aged materials are rated as more trustworthy and durable
Implicit inference: 'this material has survived; it is reliable'
justification.backing: Mikellides (1990) controlled semantic differential study. Pallasmaa (2005) existential anchoring framework. Field observation from Heerwagen (2009).
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.45 reflects empirical psychophysical ratings but limited sample diversity. CAPACITY warrant: affect effects are measured but underlying mechanisms (inferences about durability, cultural meaning) are partially inferred.
justification.rebuttal: Authenticity effect is culturally variable (see MATERIAL_CULTURAL_CONDITIONING_001 for cultural modulation). Effect size is modest; individual differences are substantial. Pristine materials may be preferred in some contexts (medical, laboratory).
competing_accounts: Aged materials are preferred due to visual novelty: refuted by preference for authentic wear over artificial distressing
Temporal depth is dispreferred in contemporary design: partially true in some markets but wabi-sabi tradition (Japan) shows opposite preference
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Mikellides empirical, Pallasmaa theoretical

mechanism_chain.process: Long-term occupancy satisfaction: buildings with natural material aging (exposed timber darkening, copper patinating, stone weathering) show UPWARD satisfaction trajectories over years; buildings with static finishes (painted, sealed, anodized) show FLAT or DOWNWARD trajectories.
mechanism_chain.source: Heerwagen (2009); informal field observation, not controlled study

data: Buildings with natural material aging show upward satisfaction trajectories over 5-10 years
Buildings with static finishes show flat or downward trajectories
Gracefully aging materials (copper patina, wood darkening) show positive aging
Ungracefully aging materials (peeling paint, yellowing plastic) show negative aging
justification.backing: Heerwagen (2009) field observations and post-occupancy evaluation data. Zuo et al. (2015) on material aging and aesthetic value. Karana et al. (2015) on emotional responses to aging.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.4 reflects field observation data but not controlled longitudinal studies. THEORETICAL_DEFAULT warrant: satisfaction trajectories are measured but confounds (occupant tenure, maintenance investment) are not fully controlled.
justification.rebuttal: Satisfaction trajectories could be confounded with occupant familiarity and habituation rather than material aging per se. Maintenance practices vary widely. Selection bias: buildings designed for natural aging may differ in other ways.
competing_accounts: Satisfaction plateaus regardless of material aging: partially true; some contexts show plateau, but natural material buildings show documented upward slopes
Aging is purely aesthetic and not functional: refuted by durability and structural benefit of graceful aging (reduced maintenance costs)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Heerwagen field authority; Karana design research

authenticity_character_boost.interpretation: Visibly aged materials are rated 0.40–0.60 standard deviations higher on authenticity and character than pristine equivalents in European cultural contexts.

satisfaction_trajectory_benefit.interpretation: Buildings with natural material aging show increasing satisfaction over time. Not quantified precisely — based on field observations rather than controlled studies.

material_aging_quality.interpretation: Not all material aging is positive. Graceful aging (patina, wear polishing, colour deepening) is evaluated positively; ungraceful aging (peeling, staining, structural degradation) is evaluated negatively. Material selection for temporal depth must prioritize gracefully aging materials.

pallasmaa_existential_anchoring.interpretation: Pallasmaa's claim that patina produces 'existential anchoring' — a sense of connection to the continuity of human habitation — is a compelling phenomenological framework but has not been empirically tested. No confidence score assigned to this parameter.

cultural_variation.effect: Temporal depth evaluation is culturally modulated. European and Japanese traditions value patina (wabi-sabi). Gulf states and some East Asian markets value pristine newness. The template must select cultural modifier before computing the temporal depth benefit.

age_of_occupant.effect: Older occupants tend to evaluate temporal depth more positively than younger occupants (possible nostalgia effect, or generational cultural difference in material preferences).

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: Temporal depth is not a direct body budget input. However, the sense of being in a well-aged, human-used environment may contribute to environmental trust and safety perception (this is a long-standing place; others have been safe here), which supports parasympathetic tone. This is speculative (confidence 0.25).
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: Temporal depth may enhance perceived control through predictability: a building that has aged gracefully communicates structural reliability and environmental stability. The occupant infers that the environment has endured and will continue to endure. This is Pallasmaa's 'existential anchoring' translated to a control variable.

cross_template_references: MATERIAL_CULTURAL_CONDITIONING_001 — cultural attitudes toward aging/patina modulate temporal depth evaluation
NATURAL_MATERIAL_CONVERGENCE_001 — natural materials age more gracefully than synthetic materials
MSI_CONGRUENCY_PRINCIPLE_001 — aged materials may produce richer multi-sensory congruency (deepened visual colour + mellowed haptic texture + aged olfactory signature)
name: Material Aging and Temporal Depth — Patina as Perceptual Enrichment

graceful_aging_material_fraction.interpretation: Fraction of building surfaces that will age gracefully (copper, bronze, natural wood, natural stone, leather). Higher fraction → more temporal depth over building lifespan → upward satisfaction trajectory.

maintenance_regime.interpretation: Over-maintenance (repainting, re-sealing, polishing away patina) prevents temporal depth accumulation. Under-maintenance (allowing structural degradation) produces ungraceful aging. Optimal: maintain structural integrity while allowing cosmetic aging.

cross_template_interactions.description: Material aging acquires cultural significance through conditioning
Patina and aging contribute to place-material identity
